Final computational report · 2026-11-13T21:07:00.955931+03:00

SpliceScore: short-read prediction of long-read splice usage

Five-cell-line assessment of junction detection, ordinal classification, continuous regression, and predictive modeling with MAJIQ and LeafCutter.

1. No ML2. Ordinal3. Continuous4. ModelsMethodology5. Dr. Gianni validation6. Differential splicing7. PSI→ΔPSI
Scope: the long-read data are the reference measurement, not an error-free biological truth. “Not observed” is depth-dependent. SpliceScore is intended to reduce and prioritize manual review, not guarantee every event without external validation.

1. Junction comparison without machine learning

This section contains no fitted model. Exact GRCh38 chromosome, intron start, intron end, and strand identifiers are compared with positive long-read junction support separately within each cell line. The combined set is the coordinate intersection detected by both MAJIQ and LeafCutter.

Model equations

Linear ridge:

y_hat = clip(0.24290759 -1.9286666e-05×majiq_raw_coverage_mean +0.00045450081×majiq_raw_coverage_sd +0.00023936026×majiq_raw_coverage_min -0.00022360004×majiq_raw_coverage_max -0.040796087×majiq_raw_coverage_usable_biological_replicates +0.59756597×majiq_raw_psi_mean_mean -0.066859756×majiq_raw_psi_mean_sd +0.16847981×majiq_raw_psi_mean_min +0.23546679×majiq_raw_psi_mean_max -0.040796087×majiq_raw_psi_mean_usable_biological_replicates +0.11994657×leafcutter_short_usage_mean +0.031092853×leafcutter_short_usage_sd -0.054433062×leafcutter_short_usage_min -0.061215304×leafcutter_short_usage_max +0×leafcutter_short_usage_usable_biological_replicates -2.6397945e-07×leafcutter_short_denominator_mean -1.3633983e-05×leafcutter_short_denominator_sd -6.3145377e-06×leafcutter_short_denominator_min +6.9257397e-06×leafcutter_short_denominator_max +0×leafcutter_short_denominator_usable_biological_replicates, 0, 1)

RBF kernel ridge:

K(x,x′)=exp[−γ‖z(x)−z(x′)‖²]
ŷ=clip(β₀+Σⱼβⱼφⱼ(z(x)),0,1)

The scalable kernel uses median imputation, standardized features, 384 seeded random Fourier features, and training-CV-selected γ and ridge α. Histogram gradient boosting is an additive tree ensemble and therefore has no single linear coefficient equation.

Detailed methodology

Inputs and coordinate matching

  1. Five cell lines: A549, HCT116, HepG2, K562, and MCF7.
  2. Technical sequencing runs belonging to the same biological replicate are summed at raw-count level.
  3. All junctions use GRCh38 0-based half-open intron coordinates plus strand. LeafCutter’s end coordinate is converted before matching.
  4. Exact junction support requires a positive long-read count in at least one biological replicate. Zero support is retained as non-observation rather than called biological absence.

Normalization

  • MAJIQ: short-read PSI is compared with long-read junction count divided by total long-read counts in the identical MAJIQ choice set/source-target context.
  • LeafCutter: junction count is divided by total junction count in the identical LeafCutter cluster, independently by biological replicate.
  • Combined: ML concatenates the allowed MAJIQ and LeafCutter predictors. No long-read count, denominator, range, error, event class, or response-derived label is a predictor.
  • CPM clarification: CPM divides by total usable library reads; it is not gene-wise normalization. Gene-junction fraction is gene-relative but only available for uniquely assigned annotated genes.
  • Biological-replicate normalized values are summarized by mean, SD, minimum, maximum, and usable-replicate count. Replicates receive equal weight; zero denominators remain NA without pseudocounts.

Training and validation

  1. A shared 55,666-row universe ensures MAJIQ-only, LeafCutter-only, and combined models are evaluated on identical junction/context rows.
  2. 45,609 rows are training and 10,057 are validation. Connected components link genes, choice sets, contexts, junctions, and LeafCutter clusters so related events do not cross the primary split.
  3. Four-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on training components selects algorithms and hyperparameters by MAE.
  4. The held-out validation split is used once for final MAE, RMSE, R², Pearson, Spearman, and error-threshold reporting.
  5. Uncertainty uses the 90th percentile of absolute out-of-fold training residuals. Ridge-versus-primary-model disagreement contributes to manual-review priority.
  6. The strict sensitivity analysis retains only events where MAJIQ choice-set and LeafCutter cluster junction membership are exactly equal.

How MAJIQ and LeafCutter are combined

In the no-ML section, combination means a simple 50:50 arithmetic consensus on common rows. In ML, combination means concatenating all ten MAJIQ summaries and ten LeafCutter summaries; the algorithm learns any weighting or nonlinear interaction exclusively from training data.

Interpretation and limitations

  • No fully independent laboratory, tissue, disease cohort, alignment protocol, or sequencing protocol has been tested.
  • Leave-one-cell-line-out testing holds out the cell line but may still expose the model to the same genes or junction identities in other cell lines.
  • The response is long-read local junction usage in a MAJIQ context, not proof of complete transcript isoform correctness.
  • LeafCutter and MAJIQ can define different denominators; use strict-sensitivity results when denominator identity is essential.
  • Bambu provenance and transcript-level Bambu validation are absent from this dataset.
  • Genome-build errors, mapping artifacts, paralogs, sample swaps, very low coverage, and novel biology may still require IGV/UCSC inspection.

5. Dr. Gianni-requested validation extension (25 November 2026)

What 100-fold CV means: 20 independently shuffled repetitions of five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold produce 100 test-fold evaluations. Related rows remain grouped by connected component. Averaging does not manufacture higher accuracy; it estimates mean performance and variability more reliably. The original held-out validation remains untouched and is still the final test.

5.2 Improving the intermediate ordinal tier

The original cumulative model recalled about 75% of intermediate MAJIQ/combined cases and 36% with LeafCutter. A training-only search compared unweighted, balanced, and middle-upweighted multinomial logistic models. Selection used 65% macro-F1 plus 35% intermediate recall, so improvement could not be obtained merely by predicting “intermediate” for everything.

Biologically, the middle tier is hardest because it contains genuinely mixed isoform usage and values near both decision boundaries. Class reweighting improves sensitivity but necessarily trades some low/high specificity; macro-F1 and both extreme recalls are therefore reported beside middle recall.

5.3 Remove A549 and HepG2 together, then test them

The new transfer model is trained only on HCT116, K562 and MCF7, then evaluated on the original held-out rows from A549 and HepG2. The “current pooled” comparator saw A549/HepG2 training partitions and is therefore an advantaged in-domain benchmark, not an external test.

5.4 Do the different logistic-regression vectors make biological sense?

Yes. The original cumulative ordinal model fits two different biological questions: vector 1 separates low usage from intermediate/high usage; vector 2 separates low/intermediate from high usage. Their standardized-weight cosine similarity is 0.985. They need not be identical because evidence that a junction is used at all can differ from evidence that it is nearly constitutive.

Interpretation rule: positive weights increase the log-odds of the named class/threshold after conditioning on all other features. MAJIQ PSI/LeafCutter usage features represent splice-choice evidence; coverage and denominator features primarily represent measurement reliability. Min/mean/max and coverage summaries are correlated, so individual coefficients are conditional associations—not causal biological effects.

5.5 Bottom line

  • Repeated grouped CV measures stability; it does not replace the held-out test or guarantee higher accuracy.
  • The middle-aware ordinal model improves intermediate recall on untouched validation while retaining explicit low/high performance reporting.
  • A549+HepG2 exclusion is a stronger cell-context transfer test than the current pooled split, but it is still internal SG-NEx validation.
  • True generalizability still requires a new laboratory/protocol or external biological cohort.

6. Differential splicing comparison

Long-read differential reference: an exact GRCh38 junction is positive only when Bambu junction |Δusage| ≥ 0.10 and the uniquely mapped gene has DEXSeq FDR ≤ 0.05 in the same cell-line comparison. The ten comparisons are analyzed separately and pooled. Bambu supplies junction effect size; DEXSeq supplies replicate-aware statistical evidence.

6.1 Junction comparison without machine learning

MAJIQ, LeafCutter and rMATS use their native significance evidence plus |ΔPSI/Δusage| ≥ 0.10. Each two-caller combination is a high-confidence consensus: both callers must call the junction differential, and evaluation is restricted to their coordinate intersection. “All three” requires at least two of three caller-specific differential calls. This section contains no fitted model.

6.2 Normalized usage agreement

Signed short-read ΔPSI/Δusage is compared directly with signed Bambu junction Δusage. Pairwise and all-three estimates are untrained arithmetic means of the available signed caller effects. MAE and RMSE measure error magnitude; R² measures identity agreement with the long-read values; Spearman measures rank agreement.

6.4 Ordinal machine learning

The data-supported ordered ΔPSI tiers are stable (<0.05), intermediate (0.05–0.10), and large (≥0.10). Models are trained on the strict all-three common universe using short-read fields only. The requested 0–0.20, 0.20–0.80 and ≥0.80 tiers remain descriptive because the ≥0.80 class has inadequate support.

6.6 Continuous-regression model comparison

Ridge, approximate RBF-kernel ridge and histogram gradient boosting were compared using grouped training-only cross-validation. The selected candidate was then evaluated once on untouched validation rows. Because this is a continuous response, MAE, RMSE, R² and Spearman—not ROC—are the primary metrics.

Interpretation boundary: the differential models estimate agreement with this Bambu+DEXSeq reference. The strict held-out all-three binary set contains very few positive junctions, so binary ML remains exploratory. Exact continuous ΔPSI regression is moderate and should not be described as a replacement for orthogonal validation.

7. PSI-calibrated-first differential splicing comparison

Pipeline: the existing SpliceScore PSI model predicts long-read-equivalent PSI independently in cell A and cell B using untouched held-out predictions. Differential usage is then calculated as predicted PSI(A) − predicted PSI(B). No long-read value from either cell enters the subtraction model, and no second-stage model is fitted on the held-out outcomes.

7.1 Exact differential-junction comparison

A PSI-derived junction is called differential when |predicted ΔPSI| ≥ 0.10, then checked against the same Bambu+DEXSeq dual reference used in Section 6. Three existing PSI models are compared: MAJIQ-only, LeafCutter-only and combined. rMATS and the seven native caller configurations remain in Section 6 because no separate rMATS-to-PSI calibration model was trained.

7.4 Ordinal machine-learning output

The underlying PSI values come from the existing ML models. Their derived |ΔPSI| is placed into the data-supported stable (<0.05), intermediate (0.05–0.10), and large (≥0.10) tiers. This evaluates transfer of the PSI model to ordinal differential splicing; it does not refit an ordinal model on the held-out outcomes.

Interpretation: this section answers whether confidence learned for individual PSI transfers to differential splicing. It should be compared with the direct ΔPSI models in Section 6, not merged with them. A future residual-correction model can use the PSI-derived ΔPSI as an input, but must be trained and tested with new leakage-controlled partitions.
